claim: Pain empathy can be evoked by observation of acute pain inflictions or facial expressions of pain.
source: Pain empathy can be evoked by multiple cues, particularly observation of acute pain inflictions or facial expressions of pain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies suggest that observation of acute pain inflictions and facial expressions of pain commonly activate the insula and anterior cingulate.
source: Previous studies suggest that these cues commonly activate the insula and anterior cingulate
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies as indicated in the abstract.

claim: Overlapping activations are not sufficient to determine process-specific shared neural representations.
source: yet vicarious pain encompasses pain-specific responses as well as unspecific processes (e.g. arousal) and overlapping activations are not sufficient to determine process-specific shared neural representations.
evidence: This is a methodological claim stated in the abstract based on theoretical considerations.

claim: Multivariate pattern analyses identified spatially and functionally similar cross-modality whole-brain vicarious pain-predictive patterns between NS and FE.
source: We employed multivariate pattern analyses to fMRI data acquired during observation of noxious stimulation of body limbs (NS) and painful facial expressions (FE) and found spatially and functionally similar cross-modality (NS versus FE) whole-brain vicarious pain-predictive patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Shared neural representations in the bilateral mid-insula were consistently identified across analyses.
source: Further analyses consistently identified shared neural representations in the bilateral mid-insula.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple analyses presented in the results.

claim: The vicarious pain patterns were not sensitive to non-painful high-arousal negative stimuli.
source: The vicarious pain patterns were not sensitive to respond to non-painful high-arousal negative stimuli but predicted self-experienced thermal pain.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's specificity analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: The vicarious pain patterns predicted self-experienced thermal pain.
source: The vicarious pain patterns were not sensitive to respond to non-painful high-arousal negative stimuli but predicted self-experienced thermal pain.
evidence: This is a finding from applying the patterns to an independent thermal pain dataset.

claim: A domain-general vicarious pain pattern predictive of self-experienced pain but not arousal was developed.
source: Finally, a domain-general vicarious pain pattern predictive of self-experienced pain but not arousal was developed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the study's pattern development.

claim: Stimuli depicting noxious stimulation of body limbs provide objective cues about the sensory component of observed pain.
source: While stimuli depicting the noxious stimulation of body limbs [i.e. observation of noxious stimulation (NS) induced vicarious pain (NS vicarious pain)] provide objective cues about the sensory component of the observed pain
evidence: This is a characterization of NS stimuli based on previous literature.

claim: Observation of facial expressions of pain is more subjective and indirect as the pain experience needs to be interpreted by the observer.
source: the observation of facial expressions of pain [i.e. facial expressions induced vicarious pain (FE vicarious pain)] is considered more subjective and indirect as the pain experience of the expresser needs to be interpreted by the observer (Hadjistavropoulos et al., 2011; Vachon-Presseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This characterization is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NS vicarious pain increased activity in core regions of the mirror neuron system, specifically inferior frontal and posterior regions.
source: For example, Vachon-Presseau et al., 2012 demonstrated that NS vicarious pain increased activity in core regions of the mirror neuron system, specifically inferior frontal and posterior regions engaged in coding sensory-somatic information (Rizzolatti and Craighero, 2004)
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited in the introduction.

claim: Presentation of facial expressions of pain led to stronger increases in the medial prefrontal cortex and precuneus.
source: while the presentation of a facial expression of pain led to stronger increases in the medial prefrontal cortex and precuneus which have been associated with social cognitive processes such as mentalizing and theory of mind (Amft et al., 2015; Gallo et al., 2018; Mitchell, 2009; Northoff et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited in the introduction.

claim: Both NS and FE stimuli elicit vicarious pain experience.
source: Despite the different psychological domains engaged in the pain empathic responses induced by NS and FE both elicit vicarious pain experience (Timmers et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous neuroimaging meta-analyses revealed that observation of acute pain infliction and painful facial expressions commonly activate the insular and cingulate cortices.
source: In line with the shared underlying mental processes previous neuroimaging meta-analyses revealed that the observation of acute pain infliction and painful facial expressions commonly activate core empathy and nociceptive pain regions specifically the insular and cingulate cortices (Jauniaux et al., 2019; Lamm et al., 2011; Timmers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple meta-analyses.

claim: Overlapping functional activations within regions do not necessarily reflect shared underlying neural representations of a specific mental process.
source: However, overlapping functional activations within these regions do not necessarily reflect shared underlying neural representations of a specific mental process (Zaki et al., 2016)
evidence: This methodological point is supported by a citation.

claim: Brain regions may contain multiple, distinct populations of neurons and averaging across those neuron populations yields nonspecific signals.
source: brain regions may contain multiple, distinct populations of neurons and averaging across those neuron populations yields nonspecific signals (Haxby et al., 2014; Zaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by citations.

claim: Electrophysiological and optogenetic studies have identified distinct neuronal populations in the anterior cingulate and insular cortices that activate during several functional domains.
source: For instance, electrophysiological and optogenetic studies have identified distinct neuronal populations in the anterior cingulate and insular cortices that activate during several functional domains, including pain- and empathy-related processes as well as attention, salience, social observation learning and reward expectancy (Allman et al., 2011; Chen, 2018; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Sakaguchi et al., 2018; Shidara and Richmond, 2002; Shura et al., 2014; Sikes and Vogt, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to electrophysiological and optogenetic studies.

claim: MVPA can be effective in extracting information at much finer spatial scales than conventional analytic approaches.
source: Compared to conventional analytic approaches, MVPA can be effective in extracting information at much finer spatial scales (e.g. below the intrinsic resolution determined by the voxel size by pooling together weak feature-selective signals in each voxel; Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Woo et al., 2017)
evidence: This methodological claim is supported by citations.

claim: MVPA represents a more suitable approach to support or reject claims about neural mechanisms that are shared between mental processes.
source: and represents a more suitable approach to support or reject claims about neural mechanisms that are shared between mental processes (Chikazoe et al., 2014; Peelen and Downing, 2007; Zaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This methodological claim is supported by citations.

claim: Using MVPA approaches, researchers have demonstrated shared neural representations across mental processes including self-experienced and observed pain in both humans and animals.
source: In support of this view, using MVPA approaches researchers have demonstrated shared neural representations across mental processes (including self-experienced and observed pain) in both humans and animals (Carrillo et al., 2019; Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2011; Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous MVPA studies.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated functional independence of overlapping univariate activation in brain regions using MVPA.
source: Moreover, a growing number of recent studies have demonstrated functional independence of overlapping univariate activation in these brain regions using MVPA (Krishnan et al., 2016; Peelen et al., 2006; Woo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent MVPA studies.

claim: Shared multivariate patterns do not necessarily imply process-specific common neural representations per se.
source: Nevertheless, shared multivariate patterns do not necessarily imply process-specific common neural representations per se given that the shared neural representations could simply reflect common demands on basal processing domains such as attention or arousal (Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2011; Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2016; Krishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This methodological consideration is supported by citations.

claim: Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2016 found shared neural patterns between vicarious and self-experienced pain in the left anterior insula that also represented disgust and unfairness.
source: For instance, Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2016 found shared neural patterns between vicarious and self-experienced pain in the left anterior insula and further demonstrated that the common local patterns were not specific to pain-related processing, but also represented disgust and unfairness suggesting modality-unspecific processing of aversive and arousing experiences.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited in the introduction.

claim: N = 238 individuals were included in the study sample.
source: we included a comparably large sample of n = 238 individuals (details see Materials and methods and Li et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample stated in the introduction.

claim: Both sets of painful stimuli were rated as considerably more painful compared to their respective control stimuli in terms of recognizing and sharing pain.
source: Affective ratings of the stimuli in an independent sample confirmed that both sets of painful stimuli were rated as considerably more painful compared to their respective control stimuli, both in terms of recognizing and sharing pain
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus validation study reported in the Results section.

claim: Both sets of painful stimuli were rated as more arousing and negative than control stimuli.
source: and additionally were rated as more arousing and negative.
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus validation study reported in the Results section.

claim: NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated with mean pain intensity displayed of 6.73 ± 0.27.
source: The NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated considerably higher on both dimensions (mean ± standard error (SE) pain intensity displayed = 6.73 ± 0.27; mean ± SE pain intensity self-experienced = 6.14 ± 0.36)
evidence: This is a specific rating value from the stimulus validation study.

claim: NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated with mean self-experienced pain intensity of 6.14 ± 0.36.
source: The NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated considerably higher on both dimensions (mean ± standard error (SE) pain intensity displayed = 6.73 ± 0.27; mean ± SE pain intensity self-experienced = 6.14 ± 0.36)
evidence: This is a specific rating value from the stimulus validation study.

claim: NS control stimuli were rated with mean pain intensity displayed of 1.37 ± 0.11.
source: as compared to the corresponding NS control stimuli (mean ± SE pain intensity displayed = 1.37 ± 0.11; mean ± SE pain intensity self-experienced = 1.54 ± 0.14; t37 = 18.11, p<0.001; t37 = 12.71, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: This is a specific rating value from the stimulus validation study.

claim: NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated significantly higher than NS control stimuli on pain intensity displayed (t37 = 18.11, p<0.001).
source: as compared to the corresponding NS control stimuli (mean ± SE pain intensity displayed = 1.37 ± 0.11; mean ± SE pain intensity self-experienced = 1.54 ± 0.14; t37 = 18.11, p<0.001; t37 = 12.71, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the stimulus validation study.

claim: FE vicarious pain stimuli were rated with mean pain intensity displayed of 6.20 ± 0.25.
source: Similarly, the FE vicarious pain stimuli were also rated substantially higher on both pain-related dimensions (mean ± SE pain intensity displayed = 6.20 ± 0.25; mean ± SE pain intensity self-experienced = 5.05 ± 0.31)
evidence: This is a specific rating value from the stimulus validation study.

claim: FE vicarious pain stimuli were rated significantly higher than FE control stimuli on pain intensity displayed (t37 = 14.58, p<0.001).
source: as compared to the corresponding FE control stimuli (mean ± SE pain intensity displayed = 1.78 ± 0.16; mean ± SE pain intensity self-experienced = 2.20 ± 0.18; t37 = 14.58, p<0.001; t37 = 9.00, p<0.001, respectively)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the stimulus validation study.

claim: NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated with mean valence of 3.14 ± 0.22.
source: Moreover, both categories of painful stimuli were rated as considerably more negative and induced stronger arousal in the participants as compared to their respective control stimuli (NS vicarious pain stimuli: mean ± SE valence=3.14 ± 0.22; mean ± SE arousal=5.81 ± 0.32
evidence: This is a specific rating value from the stimulus validation study.

claim: NS vicarious pain stimuli were rated significantly more negative than NS control stimuli (t37 = −7.99, p<0.001).
source: NS control stimuli: mean ± SE valence=5.12 ± 0.15; mean ± SE valence=2.68 ± 0.25; t37 = −7.99, p<0.001; t37 = 9.02, p<0.001, respectively
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the stimulus validation study.

claim: Activation in response to NS vicarious pain was spatially correlated with that to FE vicarious pain (r = 0.171, p<0.1).
source: We found that activation in response to NS vicarious pain was spatially correlated with that to FE vicarious pain (r = 0.171, p<0.1 based on permutation tests) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariate analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Distributed regions of overlapping activation were identified between NS and FE vicarious pain, including bilateral anterior and mid-insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, inferior parietal lobule, middle frontal gyrus and middle temporal gyrus.
source: Moreover, after multiple comparisons correction (FDR corrected, q < 0.05, two-tailed) (Figure 2B and C), distributed regions of overlapping activation were identified, including a network exhibiting increased activation during both modalities encompassing the bilateral anterior and mid-insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, inferior parietal lobule, middle frontal gyrus and middle temporal gyrus
evidence: This is a finding from the univariate analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: A network of decreased activation was identified including the rostral and ventral anterior cingulate cortices, ventromedial and orbitofrontal cortices, and lingual and parahippocampal gyri.
source: as well as a network of decreased activation, including the rostral and ventral anterior cingulate cortices, ventromedial and orbitofrontal cortices, and lingual and parahippocampal gyri (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariate analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern yielded an average classification accuracy of 88 ± 1.5% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.13.
source: The NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern yielded an average classification accuracy of 88 ± 1.5% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.13; d indicates effect size in terms of Cohen's d (accuracy = 96 ± 1.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.17 based on a two-alternative forced-choice test)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MVPA analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 80 ± 1.8% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.64.
source: and the FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 80 ± 1.8% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.64 (accuracy = 88 ± 2.1% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.57 based on a two-alternative forced-choice test)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MVPA analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The modality-specific patterns (NS and FE vicarious pain) were spatially correlated (r = 0.170, p<0.001).
source: Next, permutation-based correlation analysis was employed to determine the similarity between the whole-brain patterns of NS and FE vicarious pain which confirmed that the modality-specific patterns were spatially correlated (r = 0.170, p<0.001 based on permutation tests) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the pattern similarity analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern could reliably discriminate FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 69% accuracy (±3.0% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.65).
source: In support of this, between-modality classifications showed that the NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern could reliably discriminate FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 69% accuracy (±3.0% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.65)
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-modality prediction analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern could discriminate NS vicarious pain versus NS control with 78% accuracy (±2.7% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.00).
source: and that the FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern could discriminate NS vicarious pain versus NS control with 78% accuracy (±2.7% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.00) based on two-alternative forced-choice tests with a repeated 10-fold cross-validation procedure (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-modality prediction analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Overlapping regions in the bilateral mid-insula, left putamen and left inferior parietal lobule made reliable contributions to both NS and FE vicarious pain-predictive patterns.
source: To identify brain regions which made reliable contributions to both whole-brain NS and FE vicarious pain-predictive patterns, we thresholded the corresponding neural patterns at FDR q < 0.05 (two-tailed, bootstrap tests with 10,000 iterations) separately and found overlapping regions in the bilateral mid-insula, left putamen and left inferior parietal lobule (Figure 4A, B and C)
evidence: This is a finding from the thresholded pattern analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: A bilateral network encompassing the insula, striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex demonstrated significant within-modality cross-validation and between-modality cross-prediction accuracies.
source: We found that a bilateral network encompassing the insula, striatum as well as the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (see Figure 4D, q < 0.05, FDR corrected, two-tailed) demonstrated significant within-modality cross-validation and between-modality cross-prediction accuracies between NS and FE vicarious pain
evidence: This is a finding from the searchlight analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NS vicarious pain activation in the mid-insula was strongly positively correlated with FE vicarious pain activation (r = 0.737, p=0.006).
source: We found that NS vicarious pain activation in the insula was strongly positively correlated with FE vicarious pain activation (r = 0.737, p=0.006 based on permutation tests)
evidence: This is a finding from the mid-insula specific analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The NS vicarious pain-predictive and FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern weights within the mid-insula were strongly positively correlated (r = 0.538, p<0.001).
source: and consistent with this, that the NS vicarious pain-predictive and FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern weights within the mid-insula were also strongly positively correlated (r = 0.538, p<0.001 based on permutation tests) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the mid-insula specific analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mid-insula partial NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern classified NS vicarious pain versus NS control with 71 ± 2.9% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 0.72.
source: Consistent with the voxel-wise weight distribution two-alternative forced-choice tests revealed that the mid-insula partial NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern classified above chance for both, NS vicarious pain versus NS control (71 ± 2.9% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.72; within-modality)
evidence: This is a finding from the mid-insula partial pattern analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The mid-insula partial NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern classified FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 61 ± 3.2% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 0.36.
source: and FE vicarious pain versus FE control (61 ± 3.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.36; between-modality prediction) in out-of-sample participants through a repeated 10-fold cross-validation procedure.
evidence: This is a finding from the mid-insula partial pattern analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The mid-insula partial FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated NS vicarious pain versus NS control with 65% accuracy (±3.1% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.58).
source: In line with this, the mid-insula partial FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated NS vicarious pain versus NS control with 65% accuracy (±3.1% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.58; between-modality)
evidence: This is a finding from the mid-insula partial pattern analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The mid-insula partial FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 60% accuracy (±3.2% SE, p=0.004, d = 0.27).
source: and FE vicarious pain versus FE control with 60% accuracy (±3.2% SE, p=0.004, d = 0.27; within-modality) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the mid-insula partial pattern analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated negative versus neutral stimuli with 58 ± 3.2% accuracy, p=0.024, d = 0.34.
source: This approach revealed statistically significant yet comparably low accuracies and small effect sizes (NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern: 58 ± 3.2%, p=0.024, d = 0.34; FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern: 61 ± 3.2% SE, p=0.001, d = 0.42).
evidence: This is a finding from the specificity analysis using emotional stimuli reported in the Results section.

claim: The FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern discriminated negative versus neutral stimuli with 61 ± 3.2% SE accuracy, p=0.001, d = 0.42.
source: This approach revealed statistically significant yet comparably low accuracies and small effect sizes (NS vicarious pain-predictive pattern: 58 ± 3.2%, p=0.024, d = 0.34; FE vicarious pain-predictive pattern: 61 ± 3.2% SE, p=0.001, d = 0.42).
evidence: This is a finding from the specificity analysis using emotional stimuli reported in the Results section.

claim: Neither of the mid-insula partial patterns could classify negative stimuli above chance level.
source: In contrast, testing whether shared representations in the mid-insula could discriminate negative versus neutral stimuli revealed that neither of the insula partial patterns could classify negative stimuli above chance level (NS: 56 ± 3.2% SE, p=0.079, d = 0.11; FE: 56 ± 3.2% SE, p=0.111, d = 0.09)
evidence: This is a finding from the specificity analysis using mid-insula patterns reported in the Results section.

claim: A negative emotion-predictive pattern could accurately classify non-painful negative vs. neutral stimuli with accuracy of 86 ± 1.6% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.07.
source: In addition, using the emotional processing data we developed a negative emotion-predictive pattern which could accurately classify non-painful negative vs. neutral stimuli (accuracy = 86 ± 1.6% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.07 using a repeated 10-fold cross-validation procedure).
evidence: This is a finding from developing a negative emotion pattern reported in the Results section.

claim: The negative emotion-predictive pattern could discriminate NS vicarious pain versus its control with cross-validated accuracy of 70 ± 3.0% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.88.
source: The negative emotion-predictive pattern could significant discriminate NS vicarious pain versus its control (cross-validated accuracy = 70 ± 3.0% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.88)
evidence: This is a finding from applying the negative emotion pattern to vicarious pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The negative emotion-predictive pattern could discriminate FE vicarious pain versus its control with cross-validated accuracy of 61 ± 3.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.28.
source: and FE vicarious pain versus its control (cross-validated accuracy = 61 ± 3.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 0.28).
evidence: This is a finding from applying the negative emotion pattern to vicarious pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: Neither the whole-brain nor the mid-insula negative-predictive pattern could predict thermal pain intensity.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the pain-predictive patterns (see below for details) neither the whole-brain nor the mid-insula negative-predictive pattern could predict thermal pain intensity (whole-brain, r196 = 0.101, p=0.157; mid-insula, r196 = −0.319)
evidence: This is a finding from applying the negative emotion pattern to thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: A general vicarious pain pattern yielded a classification accuracy of 82 ± 1.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.77.
source: Given that the NS and FE vicarious pain-predictive patterns shared similar whole-brain as well as local neural representations, we developed a general vicarious pain pattern which yielded a classification accuracy of 82 ± 1.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.77 (accuracy = 91 ± 1.3% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.74 based on a two-alternative forced-choice test) in discriminating vicarious pain versus non-painful control.
evidence: This is a finding from developing the general vicarious pain pattern reported in the Results section.

claim: The general vicarious pain pattern could accurately predict NS vicarious pain from NS control with 95 ± 1.4% accuracy, p<0.001, d = 2.10.
source: More specifically, the pattern could accurately predict both NS vicarious pain from the NS control (95 ± 1.4% accuracy, p<0.001, d = 2.10)
evidence: This is a finding from testing the general vicarious pain pattern reported in the Results section.

claim: The general vicarious pain pattern could accurately predict FE vicarious pain from FE control with 87 ± 2.1% accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.45.
source: and FE vicarious pain from the FE control (87 ± 2.1% accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.45)
evidence: This is a finding from testing the general vicarious pain pattern reported in the Results section.

claim: The general vicarious pain pattern classified non-painful negative versus neutral stimuli with 59 ± 2.1% accuracy, p=0.01, d = 0.30.
source: but performed considerably worse classifying non-painful negative versus neutral stimuli (59 ± 2.1% accuracy, p=0.01, d = 0.30), in forced-choice classifications.
evidence: This is a finding from testing the general vicarious pain pattern on emotional stimuli reported in the Results section.

claim: The general vicarious pain pattern was highly similar with the NS vicarious pain pattern (r = 0.587, p<0.001).
source: In line with the spatially overlapping modality-specific vicarious pain patterns the general vicarious pain pattern was highly similar with both, the NS vicarious pain pattern (r = 0.587, permutated p<0.001 based on permutation tests)
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the general pattern to modality-specific patterns reported in the Results section.

claim: The general vicarious pain pattern was highly similar with the FE vicarious pain pattern (r = 0.702, p<0.001).
source: and FE vicarious pain pattern (r = 0.702, p<0.001 based on permutation tests).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the general pattern to modality-specific patterns reported in the Results section.

claim: The most relevant features for the general vicarious pain-predictive pattern were 'painful' and 'pain' based on Neurosynth decoding.
source: The most relevant features were 'painful' and 'pain' for the top 50 terms (excluding anatomical terms) ranked by the correlation strengths between the vicarious pain pattern and the meta-analytic maps (see word cloud, size of the font scaled by correlation strength, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic decoding analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The general vicarious pain-predictive pattern revealed a distributed network including bilateral mid-insula, inferior parietal lobule and ventromedial prefrontal cortex when thresholded at FDR q < 0.05.
source: After thresholding and correction for multiple comparisons (bootstrapping 10,000 samples, FDR q < 0.05, two-tailed), the general vicarious pain-predictive pattern revealed a distributed network engaged in vicarious pain processing encompassing the bilateral mid-insula, inferior parietal lobule and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is a finding from the thresholded general pattern analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The general vicarious pain-predictive pattern expressions were highly correlated with overall objective temperature levels (r196 = 0.538, p<0.001).
source: We found that the general vicarious pain-predictive pattern expressions were highly correlated with both overall objective temperature levels (r196 = 0.538, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from applying the general pattern to thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The general vicarious pain-predictive pattern expressions were highly correlated with subjective pain ratings (r196 = 0.507, p<0.001).
source: and subjective pain ratings (r196 = 0.507, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from applying the general pattern to thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The general pain-predictive pattern discriminated high thermal pain versus low thermal pain with 94% accuracy (±4.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.00).
source: Moreover, the general pain-predictive pattern discriminated high thermal pain versus low thermal pain with a 94% accuracy (±4.2% SE, p<0.001, d = 2.00)
evidence: This is a finding from classification tests using thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The general pain-predictive pattern discriminated high thermal pain versus medium thermal pain with 91% accuracy (±5.0% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.56).
source: high thermal pain versus medium thermal pain with a 91% accuracy (±5.0% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.56)
evidence: This is a finding from classification tests using thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The general pain-predictive pattern discriminated medium thermal pain versus low thermal pain with 82% accuracy (±6.7% SE, p=0.001, d = 1.20).
source: and medium thermal pain versus low thermal pain with an 82% accuracy (±6.7% SE, p=0.001, d = 1.20) using two-alternative forced-choice tests (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from classification tests using thermal pain data reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The mid-insula general vicarious pain-predictive local pattern could discriminate high thermal pain versus low thermal pain with 88 ± 5.7% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.56.
source: When prediction focused on the mid-insula the general vicarious pain-predictive local pattern could discriminate high thermal pain versus low thermal pain (accuracy = 88 ± 5.7% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.56)
evidence: This is a finding from mid-insula pattern classification tests using thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The mid-insula general vicarious pain-predictive local pattern could discriminate high thermal pain versus medium thermal pain with 88 ± 5.7% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.23.
source: high thermal pain versus medium thermal pain (accuracy = 88 ± 5.7% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.23)
evidence: This is a finding from mid-insula pattern classification tests using thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The mid-insula general vicarious pain-predictive local pattern could discriminate medium thermal pain versus low thermal pain with 82 ± 6.7% SE accuracy, p<0.001, d = 1.49.
source: and medium thermal pain versus low thermal pain (accuracy = 82 ± 6.7% SE, p<0.001, d = 1.49) above chance levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from mid-insula pattern classification tests using thermal pain data reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The mid-insula partial pattern expressions were highly correlated with temperature levels (r196 = 0.454, p<0.001).
source: In addition, the mid-insula partial pattern expressions (i.e. focusing on the mid-insula pattern) were highly correlated with temperature levels (r196 = 0.454, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from applying mid-insula pattern to thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The mid-insula partial pattern expressions were highly correlated with individual pain ratings (r196 = 0.440, p<0.001).
source: as well as individual pain ratings (r196 = 0.440, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from applying mid-insula pattern to thermal pain data reported in the Results section.

claim: The posterior and mid-insula receive nociceptive information from thalamic nuclei.
source: Previous non-human primate and human studies indicate that the posterior and mid-insula receive nociceptive information from thalamic nuclei (Craig et al., 1994; Craig et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Intracerebral electrical stimulation of the mid-insula evokes pain sensations.
source: Studies examining the functional and anatomical organization of the insular cortex with intracerebral electrical stimulation have demonstrated that painful sensations can be elicited by stimulation of the middle but not the anterior insula (Afif et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a stimulation study.

claim: A recent meta-analysis reported that vicarious pain uniquely activates the bilateral mid-insula and MCC as compared to empathy for non-pain negative affective states.
source: while a recent meta-analysis of conventional fMRI empathy studies reported that vicarious pain uniquely activates the bilateral mid-insula and MCC as compared to empathy for non-pain negative affective states (Timmers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The mid-insula was defined based on the Human Connectome Project multi-modal parcellation atlas encompassing PoI2, FOP2, FOP3 and MI.
source: The mid-insula was defined based on the Human Connectome Project (HCP) multi-modal parcellation atlas (Glasser et al., 2016) (encompassing PoI2, FOP2, FOP3 and MI and available from the Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience Laboratory Github repository at https://github.com/canlab/Neuroimaging_Pattern_Masks; Figure 5—figure supplement 1 displays the mid-insula mask).
evidence: This describes the anatomical definition used in the study.

claim: Small sample sizes may lead to a large cross-validation error.
source: Given that small sample sizes may lead to a large cross-validation error which is the discrepancy between the prediction accuracy measured by cross-validation and the expected accuracy on new data (Varoquaux, 2018)
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by a citation.

claim: fMRI-based inferences on regions that are most predictive substantially benefit from larger samples.
source: and fMRI-based inferences on regions that are most predictive substantially benefit from larger samples (Chang et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by a citation.

claim: N = 252 healthy young participants were enrolled in the study.
source: N = 252 healthy young participants were enrolled in the current study and underwent a previously validated NS and FE vicarious pain empathy fMRI paradigm.
evidence: This describes the initial sample size of the study.

claim: Data from 14 participants were excluded due to technical issues, left-handedness or excessive head motion.
source: Due to technical issues during data acquisition (incomplete data, n = 6), left-handedness (n = 4) or excessive head motion (>3 mm translation or 3° rotation; n = 4) data from 14 participants were excluded
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria and numbers.

claim: The final sample for pain empathy analyses included n = 238 participants (118 females; mean ± SD age=21.58 ± 2.32 years).
source: leading to a sample of n = 238 participants (118 females; mean ± SD age=21.58 ± 2.32 years) for the pain empathy analyses
evidence: This describes the final sample characteristics.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee at the University of Electronic Science and Technology and was in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: Participants provided written consent, the study was approved by the ethics committee at the University of Electronic Science and Technology and was in accordance the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Thirty-three healthy subjects participated in the thermal pain study.
source: Thirty-three healthy (22 females; mean ± SD age=27.9 ± 9.0 years), right-handed subjects participated in the thermal pain study (details see Wager et al., 2013; Woo et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the sample for the independent thermal pain dataset.

claim: Six levels of temperature ranging from 44.3°C to 49.3°C in increments of 1°C were delivered in the thermal pain study.
source: Six levels of temperature (ranging from 44.3°C to 49.3°C in increments of 1°C) were delivered to the volar surface of the left inner forearm using a TSA-II Neurosensory Analyzer (Medoc Ltd.) with a 16 mm Peltier thermode end-plate during fMRI acquisition.
evidence: This describes the thermal pain stimulation parameters.
